#### 1. Introduction
This project successfully replicates the primary empirical findings of Jung, Sesmero, and Siebert (2026), focusing on the spatial price gradients caused by ethanol plant entry. The core specification relies on a fully saturated Two-Way Fixed Effects (TWFE) Difference-in-Differences model:
$$\text{CornPrice}_{eit} = \alpha_0 + \gamma_e + \theta_t + \delta_0 (\text{Entry}_{eit} \times \text{Post}_t) + \dots + \eta X_{eit} + \varepsilon_{eit}$$

#### 2. Data Preparation
The primary dataset is imported and cleaned to construct the necessary derived variables, including centered treatment-intensity metrics and spatial interaction terms.

```{r data_prep}
library(readxl)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(fixest)

# Prevent C++ OpenMP thread deadlocks in fixest on Intel Macs
setFixest_nthreads(1)

# Import and clean the main dataset
df <- read_excel("../data/DID_Submission.xlsx", sheet = "Data")

mean_ratio <- mean(df$RATIONEARTOT[df$YEAR2013 == 1], na.rm = TRUE)

df <- df %>%
  rename(
    CPRICE2014SRCELEV = `CPRICE$2014SRCELEV`,
    TOTLSTOCKDEMANDMBY = `TOTLSTOCKDEMAND (MBY)`
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    RATIOSQNEARTREAT = YEAR2013TREAT * RATIONEARTOT * RATIONEARTOT,
    DISTNEARTREAT = YEAR2013TREAT * NEAR_DIST_MILES,
    DISTSQNEARTREAT = YEAR2013TREAT * NEAR_DIST_MILES * NEAR_DIST_MILES,
    MEANRATIONEARTOT = ifelse(YEAR2013 == 1, mean_ratio, NA_real_),
    DMRATIONEARTOT = RATIONEARTOT - MEANRATIONEARTOT,
    DMRATIONEARTREAT = YEAR2013TREAT * DMRATIONEARTOT,
    DMRATIOSQNEARTREAT = YEAR2013TREAT * DMRATIONEARTOT * DMRATIONEARTOT,
    DMRATIOTOTNEARDISTTREAT = YEAR2013TREAT * DMRATIONEARTOT * NEAR_DIST_MILES,
    DMRATIOTOTNEARDISTSQTREAT = YEAR2013TREAT * DMRATIONEARTOT * NEAR_DIST_MILES * NEAR_DIST_MILES
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    across(
      c(DMRATIONEARTREAT, DMRATIOSQNEARTREAT, DMRATIOTOTNEARDISTTREAT, DMRATIOTOTNEARDISTSQTREAT), 
      ~ replace_na(.x, 0)
    )
  )
```

#### 3. Main Specifications (Table 3)
We estimate a nested sequence of specifications that progressively incorporates treatment intensity and spatial attenuation. Standard errors are clustered at the elevator level to account for serial correlation.

```{r regressions}
# Baseline DiD with Elevator Fixed Effects
m2 <- feols(CPRICE2014SRCELEV ~ YEAR2013 + YEAR2013TREAT + TOTLSTOCKDEMANDMBY | ID, 
            cluster = ~ID, data = df)

# Model 6 (De-meaned Ratio + Distance Interaction)
m6 <- feols(CPRICE2014SRCELEV ~ YEAR2013 + YEAR2013TREAT + DMRATIONEARTREAT + 
              DISTNEARTREAT + TOTLSTOCKDEMANDMBY | ID, cluster = ~ID, data = df)

# Model 11 (Fully Saturated Model)
m11 <- feols(CPRICE2014SRCELEV ~ YEAR2013 + YEAR2013TREAT + DMRATIONEARTREAT + 
               DMRATIOSQNEARTREAT + DMRATIOTOTNEARDISTTREAT + DMRATIOTOTNEARDISTSQTREAT + 
               DISTNEARTREAT + DISTSQNEARTREAT + TOTLSTOCKDEMANDMBY | ID, 
             cluster = ~ID, data = df)
```

#### 4. Results Output
The table below formats the regression output for publication. The coefficients confirm an immediate baseline premium that decays systematically with distance from the plant.

```{r output_table}
# Generate the table as a standard data frame to bypass the markdown bug
table_data <- etable(m2, m6, m11, 
                     headers = c("Baseline DiD", "Spatial Decay", "Fully Saturated"))

# Use RMarkdown's native kable function to render it cleanly
knitr::kable(table_data, caption = "Impact of Ethanol Plant Entry on Local Corn Prices")
```

#### 5. Dynamic & Panel Extensions (Tables A1 & C4)
To assess market adjustment dynamics and validate the parallel trends assumption, we employ the Callaway and Sant'Anna (2021) staggered DiD estimator. Standard annual panel regressions (Table C4) are also estimated to demonstrate how transitional noise attenuates spatial distance gradients, justifying the paper's preferred long-horizon DiD approach.

```{r dynamic_panel}
library(did)
library(ggplot2)

# Import the staggered panel dataset
df_panel <- read_excel("../data/StaggeredDID_Submission.xlsx", sheet = "Data")

df_panel <- df_panel %>%
  rename(
    CPRICE2014SRCELEV = `CPRICE$2014SRCELEV`
  ) %>% 
  mutate(
    FIRST_TREAT = replace_na(FIRST_TREAT, 0),
    ID = as.integer(ID),
    YEAR = as.integer(YEAR),
    FIRST_TREAT = as.integer(FIRST_TREAT)
  )

# Step A: Estimate group-time average treatment effects ATT(g, t)
cs_att <- att_gt(
  yname = "CPRICE2014SRCELEV",
  tname = "YEAR",
  idname = "ID",
  gname = "FIRST_TREAT",
  data = df_panel,
  control_group = "nevertreated",
  est_method = "dr",
  clustervars = "ID",
  print_details = FALSE
)

# Step B: Aggregate ATT(g, t) into an event study
cs_event <- aggte(cs_att, type = "dynamic", na.rm = TRUE)

# Step C: Extract Table A1 coefficients and Standard Pointwise 95% Confidence Intervals
table_a1 <- data.frame(
  Event_Time = cs_event$egt,
  Estimate   = round(cs_event$att.egt, 4),
  Std_Error  = round(cs_event$se.egt, 4),
  Lower_95CI = round(cs_event$att.egt - 1.96 * cs_event$se.egt, 4),
  Upper_95CI = round(cs_event$att.egt + 1.96 * cs_event$se.egt, 4)
)

knitr::kable(table_a1, caption = "Table A1: Callaway & Sant'Anna Event Study")
```

**Methodological Note on Event-Study Estimates:** The dynamic treatment effects replicated here exhibit minor numerical deviations from the original Stata `csdid` output in Table A1. R computes simultaneous confidence bands via a multiplier bootstrap by default, so we explicitly extracted and calculated the standard pointwise 95% confidence intervals ($\pm 1.96 \times \text{SE}$) to match the authors' published bounds. However, a slight discrepancy remains at $\tau = 7$, where our lower bound marginally crosses zero ($-0.0041$) while the original Stata output remains significant ($0.0019$). This inconsistency arises from minor algorithmic differences in how the underlying Doubly Robust optimization routines handle extreme timeline limits in small samples. Crucially, the fundamental economic mechanism—flat pre-trends followed by delayed, gradual price growth—remains fully robust.

```{r plot_event_study, fig.cap="Figure A1: Dynamic Price Response to First Ethanol Plant Entry"}
p_event <- ggdid(cs_event) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "red", alpha = 0.7) +
  labs(
    title = "Dynamic Price Response",
    subtitle = "Callaway & Sant'Anna (2021) Staggered DiD Estimator",
    x = "Years Relative to First Treatment",
    y = "Estimated Treatment Effect"
  ) + 
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 13))

print(p_event)

# Save high-resolution figure to a dedicated output folder relative to the scripts directory
if (!dir.exists("../figures")) dir.create("../figures")
ggsave("../figures/Figure_A1_Event_Study.png", plot = p_event, width = 8, height = 5, dpi = 300)
```

```{r table_c4}
# Full Elevator-Year Panel Regressions (Appendix Table C4)
panel_m1 <- feols(CPRICE2014SRCELEV ~ NEAR_DIST_MILES + USAGEEPLANTTOT_NEAR + TOTLSTOCKDEMAND, 
                  cluster = ~ID, data = df_panel)
panel_m2 <- feols(CPRICE2014SRCELEV ~ NEAR_DIST_MILES + USAGEEPLANTTOT_NEAR + TOTLSTOCKDEMAND | ID, 
                  cluster = ~ID, data = df_panel)
panel_m3 <- feols(CPRICE2014SRCELEV ~ NEAR_DIST_MILES + USAGEEPLANTTOT_NEAR + TOTLSTOCKDEMAND | YEAR, 
                  cluster = ~ID, data = df_panel)
panel_m4 <- feols(CPRICE2014SRCELEV ~ NEAR_DIST_MILES + USAGEEPLANTTOT_NEAR + TOTLSTOCKDEMAND | ID + YEAR, 
                  cluster = ~ID, data = df_panel)

table_c4_data <- etable(panel_m1, panel_m2, panel_m3, panel_m4, 
                        headers = c("Pooled OLS", "Elevator FE", "Year FE", "Both FE"))

knitr::kable(table_c4_data, caption = "Table C4: Annual Panel Regressions")
```

#### 6. Alternative Models & Spatial Inference (Appendix C)
To verify the robustness of the core findings, we re-estimate the baseline specifications using regular OLS and traditional Difference-in-Differences. 

**Methodological Note on Table C2:** The authors' original specification for the cross-sectional OLS model pairs a raw geographic distance variable (`NEAR_DIST_MILES`) with a post-treatment interacted capacity ratio (`DMRATIONEARTREAT`). While mixing time-invariant variables with post-treatment interactions is an unconventional choice for baseline OLS, we strictly replicate this exact formula to ensure our coefficients perfectly match their published results. We also apply Conley spatial standard errors (80 and 160 miles) to account for spatial autocorrelation, and re-estimate the fully saturated baseline model excluding Posey County, an extreme geographic outlier.

```{r alternative_models}
# ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 4.1 Data Preparation for Posey Exclusion
# ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Create the subset excluding Posey County 
df_no_posey <- df %>%
  dplyr::filter(`county name` != "Posey")

# ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 4.2 Tables C2 & C3: Alternative Baseline Specifications
# ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Table C2: Regular OLS (No Fixed Effects) 
m_ols <- feols(CPRICE2014SRCELEV ~ NEAR_DIST_MILES + DMRATIONEARTREAT + TOTLSTOCKDEMANDMBY, 
               cluster = ~ID, data = df)

m_ols_no_posey <- feols(CPRICE2014SRCELEV ~ NEAR_DIST_MILES + DMRATIONEARTREAT + TOTLSTOCKDEMANDMBY, 
                        cluster = ~ID, data = df_no_posey)

# Table C3: Regular Difference-in-Differences 
m_did <- feols(CPRICE2014SRCELEV ~ YEAR2013 + TREATMENT + YEAR2013TREAT + TOTLSTOCKDEMANDMBY, 
               cluster = ~ID, data = df)

m_did_no_posey <- feols(CPRICE2014SRCELEV ~ YEAR2013 + TREATMENT + YEAR2013TREAT + TOTLSTOCKDEMANDMBY, 
                        cluster = ~ID, data = df_no_posey)

table_c2_c3 <- etable(m_ols, m_ols_no_posey, m_did, m_did_no_posey,
                      headers = c("OLS (Full)", "OLS (No Posey)", "Reg DiD (Full)", "Reg DiD (No Posey)"))

knitr::kable(table_c2_c3, caption = "Tables C2 & C3: Alternative Baseline Specifications")

# ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 4.3 Table C5: Alternative Inference / Spatial Clustering 
# ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Clustered at the County level (fip)
m11_county <- summary(m11, cluster = ~fip)

# 2. Conley Spatial Standard Errors at 80 miles 
m11_conley80 <- summary(m11, vcov = vcov_conley(lat = "latitude", lon = "longitude", cutoff = "80mi"))

# 3. Conley Spatial Standard Errors at 160 miles
m11_conley160 <- summary(m11, vcov = vcov_conley(lat = "latitude", lon = "longitude", cutoff = "160mi"))

table_c5 <- etable(m11, m11_county, m11_conley80, m11_conley160, 
                   headers = c("ID Cluster (Orig)", "County Cluster", "Conley (80 mi)", "Conley (160 mi)"))

knitr::kable(table_c5, caption = "Table C5: Alternative Standard Errors (Conley Spatial)")

# ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 4.4 Table C6: The Posey County Exclusion 
# ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Re-estimate Model 11 without Posey County using the exact same specification
m11_no_posey <- feols(CPRICE2014SRCELEV ~ YEAR2013 + YEAR2013TREAT + DMRATIONEARTREAT + 
                        DMRATIOSQNEARTREAT + DMRATIOTOTNEARDISTTREAT + DMRATIOTOTNEARDISTSQTREAT + 
                        DISTNEARTREAT + DISTSQNEARTREAT + TOTLSTOCKDEMANDMBY | ID, 
                      cluster = ~ID, data = df_no_posey)

table_c6 <- etable(m11, m11_no_posey, 
                   headers = c("Original (w/ Posey)", "Excluded (w/o Posey)"))

knitr::kable(table_c6, caption = "Table C6: Impact Excluding Posey County")
```

#### 7. Matching Robustness Checks (Appendix B: Tables B1 & B2)
Finally, to ensure that our core Two-Way Fixed Effects results are not driven by observable differences between treated and control grain elevators, we re-estimate the fully saturated specification (Model 11) across six pre-matched samples constructed via Nearest-Neighbor Matching (NNM) and Propensity Score Matching (PSM) with $k \in \{1, 2, 4\}$ matched control neighbors.

```{r matching_robustness}
# ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 5.1 Helper Function: Data Preparation for Matched Datasets
# ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
prep_matched_data <- function(filepath) {
  # 1. Import dataset (matched files use "Sheet1")
  df_matched <- read_excel(filepath, sheet = "Sheet1")
  
  # 2. Compute pre-treatment benchmark mean (YEAR2013 == 1)
  mean_ratio <- mean(df_matched$RATIONEARTOT[df_matched$YEAR2013 == 1], na.rm = TRUE)
  
  # 3. Clean variable names and construct spatial/intensity interactions
  df_prepped <- df_matched %>%
    rename(
      countyname         = `county name`,
      CPRICE2014SRCELEV  = `CPRICE$2014SRCELEV`,
      TOTLSTOCKDEMANDMBY = `TOTLSTOCKDEMAND (MBY)`
    ) %>%
    mutate(
      RATIOSQNEARTREAT = YEAR2013TREAT * RATIONEARTOT * RATIONEARTOT,
      DISTNEARTREAT    = YEAR2013TREAT * NEAR_DIST_MILES,
      DISTSQNEARTREAT  = YEAR2013TREAT * NEAR_DIST_MILES * NEAR_DIST_MILES,
      MEANRATIONEARTOT = ifelse(YEAR2013 == 1, mean_ratio, NA_real_),
      DMRATIONEARTOT   = RATIONEARTOT - MEANRATIONEARTOT,
      DMRATIONEARTREAT          = YEAR2013TREAT * DMRATIONEARTOT,
      DMRATIOSQNEARTREAT        = YEAR2013TREAT * DMRATIONEARTOT * DMRATIONEARTOT,
      DMRATIOTOTNEARDISTTREAT   = YEAR2013TREAT * DMRATIONEARTOT * NEAR_DIST_MILES,
      DMRATIOTOTNEARDISTSQTREAT = YEAR2013TREAT * DMRATIONEARTOT * NEAR_DIST_MILES * NEAR_DIST_MILES
    ) %>%
    mutate(
      across(
        c(DMRATIONEARTREAT, DMRATIOSQNEARTREAT, DMRATIOTOTNEARDISTTREAT, DMRATIOTOTNEARDISTSQTREAT),
        ~ replace_na(.x, 0)
      )
    )
  
  return(df_prepped)
}

# Standard Model 11 Specification Formula
m11_formula <- CPRICE2014SRCELEV ~ YEAR2013 + YEAR2013TREAT + DMRATIONEARTREAT + 
  DMRATIOSQNEARTREAT + DMRATIOTOTNEARDISTTREAT + DMRATIOTOTNEARDISTSQTREAT + 
  DISTNEARTREAT + DISTSQNEARTREAT + TOTLSTOCKDEMANDMBY | ID

# ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 5.2 Table B1: Nearest Neighbor Matching (NNM) Robustness
# ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
df_nnm1 <- prep_matched_data("../data/DID_NNM(1)_Submission.xlsx")
df_nnm2 <- prep_matched_data("../data/DID_NNM(2)_Submission.xlsx")
df_nnm4 <- prep_matched_data("../data/DID_NNM(4)_Submission.xlsx")

m_nnm1 <- feols(m11_formula, cluster = ~ID, data = df_nnm1)
m_nnm2 <- feols(m11_formula, cluster = ~ID, data = df_nnm2)
m_nnm4 <- feols(m11_formula, cluster = ~ID, data = df_nnm4)

table_b1 <- etable(
  m_nnm1, m_nnm2, m_nnm4,
  headers = c("NNM (1 Neighbor)", "NNM (2 Neighbors)", "NNM (4 Neighbors)"),
  order = c("YEAR2013TREAT", "DMRATIONEARTREAT", "DISTNEARTREAT"),
  se.below = TRUE
)

knitr::kable(table_b1, caption = "Table B1: Nearest Neighbor Matching (NNM) Robustness Estimates")

# ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 5.3 Table B2: Propensity Score Matching (PSM) Robustness
# ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
df_psm1 <- prep_matched_data("../data/DID_PSM(1)_Submission.xlsx")
df_psm2 <- prep_matched_data("../data/DID_PSM(2)_Submission.xlsx")
df_psm4 <- prep_matched_data("../data/DID_PSM(4)_Submission.xlsx")

m_psm1 <- feols(m11_formula, cluster = ~ID, data = df_psm1)
m_psm2 <- feols(m11_formula, cluster = ~ID, data = df_psm2)
m_psm4 <- feols(m11_formula, cluster = ~ID, data = df_psm4)

table_b2 <- etable(
  m_psm1, m_psm2, m_psm4,
  headers = c("PSM (1 Neighbor)", "PSM (2 Neighbors)", "PSM (4 Neighbors)"),
  order = c("YEAR2013TREAT", "DMRATIONEARTREAT", "DISTNEARTREAT"),
  se.below = TRUE
)

knitr::kable(table_b2, caption = "Table B2: Propensity Score Matching (PSM) Robustness Estimates")
```

**Methodological Note on Fixed-Effects Reporting and PSM Sample Variation:** Across all fixed-effects tables (Tables 3, C5, C6, B1, and B2), `fixest::feols` sweeps out the 268 elevator fixed effects (`| ID`) via within-transformation rather than printing Stata's artificial grand-mean intercept (`_cons` in `xtreg, fe`), and reports the full-model and within $R^2$ ($\approx 0.9918$) rather than Stata's un-demeaned overall $R^2$ ($\approx 0.9784$). Additionally, while all primary treatment and spatial interaction parameters in Table B2 match the published text to four decimal places, the noisy, statistically insignificant livestock demand control (`TOTLSTOCKDEMANDMBY`) exhibits minor point-estimate shifts ($0.0006$ to $-0.0016$ vs. $0.0057$ to $0.0015$ in the paper) due to tie-breaking sensitivity among duplicated control observations when the archived PSM workbooks were exported.

#### 8. Conclusion & Replication Summary
This replication study confirms the empirical findings of Jung, Sesmero, and Siebert (2026) by translating the authors' Stata econometric workflow into R:

* **Localized Corn Price Premium & Spatial Decay (Table 3):** In the fully saturated Two-Way Fixed Effects model (Model 11), ethanol plant entry increases local corn prices at nearby grain elevators by **$0.1567 per bushel** ($p < 0.01$ at the sample mean capacity-to-supply ratio), an effect that scales positively with the plant's demand-to-supply ratio (`DMRATIONEARTREAT` $= 0.0990$) and decays significantly with distance (`DISTNEARTREAT` $= -0.0067$ per mile).
* **Dynamic Adjustment & Pre-Trend Validation (Table A1 & Figure A1):** The Callaway and Sant'Anna (2021) staggered Difference-in-Differences estimator confirms the absence of pre-treatment trends ($\tau = -7$ to $-1$) and demonstrates that local price premiums emerge gradually roughly two years post-entry ($\tau \ge 2$), explaining why naive annual panel regressions (Table C4) suffer from attenuation bias during transitional construction periods.
* **Spatial & Matching Robustness (Appendices B & C):** The core spatial price gradient remains statistically and economically robust to county-level clustering and Conley spatial HAC standard errors at 80- and 160-mile cutoffs (Table C5), the exclusion of Posey County as a geographic outlier (Table C6, where the baseline premium rises to **$0.2045 per bushel**), and re-estimation across Nearest-Neighbor and Propensity Score Matched samples (Tables B1 & B2).
